newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss private bank chases West European shares.
newsitem.headline: Swiss private bank chases West European shares.

text.p: Swiss private bank Union Bancaire Privee said West European stocks had become a favourite destination for asset allocation, offering strong earnings prospects thanks to corporate restructuring.
With low inflation and a favourable interest rate climate, equities in Europe offered even richer pickings than emerging markets, the bank's investment manager Marc Polydor said.

"We don't see emerging markets booming, asset managers are becoming defensive about them. There's so much good potential and visibility now in European corporate restructuring, we don't see a need to go much into emerging markets," he told Reuters.

"In Europe, earnings will rise, there'll be a lot of investment opportunities. It's just next door -- why should I go and buy something in Russia?," said Polydor, Union Bancaire Privee's chief strategist and a member of senior management.
Polydor said the bank was favouring German car maker Daimler Benz, pharmaceuticals group Bayer and chemicals group Hoechst, which has revealed plans to restructure under a holding company.
"The German market remains cheap and there is a prospective of ongoing restructuring," Polydor said.

Elsewhere, the Netherlands' ING Bank and supermarkets group Ahold and Switzerland's pharmaceuticals firms Roche and Novartis were attracting attention. But the bank was concerned about British equities because of prospects of interest rate rises.
In Asia, Union Bancaire Privee recently increased its exposure to Hong Kong equities, which makes up about four percent of the total stock portfolio, Polydor said.

"Hong Kong is one of our main bets in Asia. The Hong Kong market is very under-valued, the earnings are there," he said. "We don't believe there'll be any major changes in Hong Kong after the Chinese takeover (in July 1997)."
Polydor said the bank was cautious about U.S. markets amid signs of an economic slowdown and recently raised cash exposure in its U.S. investment portfolio at the expense of bonds.

"The visibility is quite good for the U.S. market until January and we're maintaining our fixed income bond exposure. But if we see risks in the U.S. market in mid-January, we may reduce our bond maturities or increase cash," he said.
The bank's medium-risk dollar portfolio allocated roughly 45 percent in equities and stocks, 30 in bonds and 25 in cash.
Its medium-risk Swiss franc portfolio allocated 45 percent in equities, 45 percent in bonds -- majority Swiss and some German -- and 10 percent in cash.
